> **What you can defend when you leave.** Decide how you and your tools will work before there is anything at stake, so the rules exist when the pressure arrives.

## What this station produces

A responsibility statement naming what you will never delegate, your AI and data-handling rules, your opened AI Research Ledger, and an early red-flag screen of your project idea.

This is a **versioned checkpoint**, not a pass. You date it, number it, and
attach the reason for the version. When later evidence changes it, you write
the next version rather than editing the last one, because the sequence of
changes is itself part of your research record.

## The practice

1. {'Write your responsibility statement': 'the decisions that stay yours no matter how good the tool gets.'}
2. {'Write your AI working rules': 'what you will delegate, what you will always verify, and how you will record both.'}
3. Open your AI Research Ledger and enter your first row, today, for any tool you have already used on this project.
4. {'Run the red-flag screen on your idea': 'is it answerable, is it yours to ask, and could you defend attempting it.'}

## The four rails, here

Four concerns cross every station in this book. At this station they take
these specific forms.

- **Ethics, permissions, and data exposure.** State now what data you expect to touch, so the ethics station has something to check against.
- **Evidence, provenance, and reproducibility.** Decide where your project's files will live before you have any.
- **AI activity, verification, and human decisions.** This station opens the ledger every other station appends to.
- **Uncertainty, claim boundary, and revision history.** Write what you currently believe about your question, so later revisions are visible as revisions.

## What sends you back

Any change in your tools, your data source, or your collaborators sends you back here for a new version.
